claim: Hair cells express two isoforms of myosin 15 that differ by inclusion of an 133-kDa N-terminal domain.
source: We found that hair cells express two isoforms of myosin 15 that differ by inclusion of an 133-kDa N-terminal domain, and that these isoforms can selectively traffic to different stereocilia rows.
evidence: Supported by qPCR data showing expression of both isoforms (Figure 1E-G), immunofluorescence showing differential localization (Figure 3), and molecular characterization of the isoforms (Figure 1A).

claim: Myosin 15 isoforms can selectively traffic to different stereocilia rows.
source: We found that hair cells express two isoforms of myosin 15 that differ by inclusion of an 133-kDa N-terminal domain, and that these isoforms can selectively traffic to different stereocilia rows.
evidence: Demonstrated by immunofluorescence showing isoform 1 localizes to shorter row stereocilia (Figure 3A,B) while isoform 2 localizes to tallest row (Figure 4A,B).

claim: Hair cells expressing only the small isoform develop normal stereocilia bundles.
source: Using an isoform-specific knockout mouse, we show that hair cells expressing only the small isoform remarkably develop normal stereocilia bundles.
evidence: Demonstrated by SEM showing normal staircase architecture in Myo15ΔN/ΔN hair cells at P4 (Figure 2A,B).

claim: A critical subset of stereocilia with active mechanotransducer channels subsequently retracts in isoform 1-null mice.
source: However, a critical subset of stereocilia with active mechanotransducer channels subsequently retracts.
evidence: Shown by SEM of Myo15ΔN/ΔN hair cells at P32 and P50 showing selective degeneration of shorter row stereocilia (Figure 6A,B).

claim: The larger isoform with the 133-kDa N-terminal domain traffics to specialized stereocilia and prevents disassembly of their actin core.
source: The larger isoform with the 133-kDa N-terminal domain traffics to these specialized stereocilia and prevents disassembly of their actin core.
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence showing isoform 1 localization to shorter rows (Figure 3A,B) and TEM showing actin core disassembly in isoform 1-null mice (Figure 7C-F).

claim: Myo15ΔN/ΔN mice are profoundly deaf at all frequencies tested at 6 weeks of age.
source: Myo15ΔN/ΔN mice were profoundly deaf at all frequencies tested (Figure 1B).
evidence: ABR thresholds exceeded 100 dB SPL at 4, 20, and 48 kHz in 6-week-old Myo15ΔN/ΔN mice (Figure 1B).

claim: Myo15ΔN/ΔN mice respond to loud sounds of 75 dB SPL at 20 kHz at 2 weeks of age.
source: However, around the onset of hearing at 2 weeks, Myo15ΔN/ΔN mice did respond to loud sounds of 75 dB of sound pressure level (dB SPL) at 20 kHz, the most sensitive frequency range of mouse hearing (Figure 1C).
evidence: ABR measurements at 2 weeks showing responses at 75 dB SPL (Figure 1C).

claim: By 4 and 6 weeks of age ABR thresholds at 20 kHz exceeded 100 dB SPL in Myo15ΔN/ΔN mice.
source: However, by 4 and 6 weeks of age ABR thresholds at 20 kHz exceeded 100 dB SPL in Myo15ΔN/ΔN mice, indicating a rapid progression to profound deafness (Figure 1C).
evidence: ABR measurements showing thresholds >100 dB SPL at 4 and 6 weeks (Figure 1C).

claim: There is a complete absence of DPOAEs in Myo15ΔN/ΔN mice at 6 weeks of age.
source: There was a complete absence of DPOAEs in Myo15ΔN/ΔN mice at 2 weeks (data not shown) and 6 weeks of age (Figure 1D), where in contrast Myo15+/+ littermates had normal DPOAEs at 2 weeks (data not shown) and 6 weeks (Figure 1D).
evidence: DPOAE measurements showing no emissions in Myo15ΔN/ΔN mice at 6 weeks (Figure 1D).

claim: Cochlear amplification is disrupted in Myo15ΔN/ΔN mice.
source: We conclude that cochlear amplification is disrupted in Myo15ΔN/ΔN mice, and that this contributes to the profound deafness evident by 4 weeks of age.
evidence: Inferred from absence of DPOAEs which measure outer hair cell function (Figure 1D).

claim: Myo15ΔN/ΔN mice lack circling behavior and perform normally in swimming tests.
source: Myo15ΔN/ΔN mice lacked circling behavior and performed normally in swimming tests (data not shown).
evidence: Behavioral observations of vestibular function.

claim: Myo15sh2/sh2 and Myo15sh2-J/sh2-J mice have profound congenital deafness and vestibular dysfunction typified by persistent head bobbing and circling behaviors.
source: Myo15sh2/sh2 and Myo15sh2-J/sh2-J mice have profound congenital deafness and vestibular dysfunction typified by persistent head bobbing and circling behaviors (Probst et al., 1998; Anderson et al., 2000).
evidence: Referenced from prior publications (Probst et al., 1998; Anderson et al., 2000).

claim: Total pool of Myo15 transcripts remained stable between P0 and P21.
source: The total pool of Myo15 transcripts remained stable between P0 and P21 (Figure 1E), but this concealed an underlying switch in exon 2 splicing.
evidence: qPCR measurements of motor domain transcripts common to both isoforms (Figure 1E).

claim: Transcripts encoding isoform 1 became progressively more abundant, increasing ∼nine-fold from P0 through to P21.
source: Transcripts encoding isoform 1 became progressively more abundant, increasing ∼nine-fold from P0 through to P21 (Figure 1F and Figure 1—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: qPCR measurements of exon 2-3 junction transcripts (Figure 1F).

claim: The amount of isoform 2 sharply decreased ∼21-fold between P0 and P6 and remained stable thereafter.
source: Conversely, the amount of isoform 2 sharply decreased ∼21-fold between P0 and P6 and remained stable thereafter (Figure 1G and Figure 1—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: qPCR measurements of exon 1-3 junction transcripts (Figure 1G).

claim: The p.E1086X mutation did not induce nonsense mediated mRNA decay or change the relative abundance of isoform transcripts.
source: These data show that the p.E1086X mutation did not induce nonsense mediated mRNA decay or change the relative abundance of isoform transcripts.
evidence: qPCR showing no significant difference in transcript levels between Myo15+/ΔN and Myo15ΔN/ΔN at P0 (Figure 1H).

claim: Isoform 2 mRNA was predominantly expressed during early neonatal development.
source: We conclude that isoform 2 mRNA was predominantly expressed during early neonatal development, but that alternative splicing progressively shifts to favor isoform 1 in postnatal cochleae.
evidence: qPCR data showing high isoform 2 at P0 and decline thereafter (Figure 1G).

claim: Alternative splicing progressively shifts to favor isoform 1 in postnatal cochleae.
source: We conclude that isoform 2 mRNA was predominantly expressed during early neonatal development, but that alternative splicing progressively shifts to favor isoform 1 in postnatal cochleae.
evidence: qPCR data showing increase in isoform 1 from P0 to P21 (Figure 1F).

claim: Stereocilia bundles of Myo15ΔN/ΔN inner hair cells had the characteristic staircase architecture and were indistinguishable from normal hearing Myo15+/ΔN littermate controls at P4.
source: Remarkably, unlike the short stereocilia bundles of Myo15sh2/sh2 and Myo15sh2-J/sh2-J hair cells (Probst et al., 1998; Anderson et al., 2000), we found that stereocilia bundles of Myo15ΔN/ΔN inner hair cells (IHCs) had the characteristic staircase architecture and were indistinguishable from normal hearing Myo15+/ΔN littermate controls at P4 (Figure 2A).
evidence: SEM images showing normal staircase architecture in Myo15ΔN/ΔN IHCs at P4 (Figure 2A).

claim: There were no differences in either the distribution of heights or the aspect ratio of the second row mechanosensitive stereocilia tips between Myo15ΔN/ΔN and control Myo15+/ΔN IHC bundles at P4.
source: We quantified the architecture of Myo15ΔN/ΔN and control Myo15+/ΔN IHC bundles at P4 and found no differences in either the distribution of heights (Figure 7—figure supplement 2), or the aspect ratio of the second row mechanosensitive stereocilia tips (Figure 7—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Quantitative morphometric analysis of stereocilia heights and tip shapes (Figure 7—figure supplements 2, 3).

claim: Tip-links were present in both Myo15ΔN/ΔN and Myo15+/ΔN IHCs at P4.
source: Tip-links were present in both Myo15ΔN/ΔN and Myo15+/ΔN IHCs (Figure 2A, lower panels).
evidence: SEM images showing tip-links in both genotypes (Figure 2A).

claim: Hair bundles of Myo15sh2/sh2 IHCs had supernumerary stereocilia rows, which were not observed in Myo15ΔN/ΔN IHCs.
source: Hair bundles of Myo15sh2/sh2 IHCs also had supernumerary stereocilia rows, which were not observed in Myo15ΔN/ΔN IHCs (Figure 2A).
evidence: SEM comparison showing additional rows in Myo15sh2/sh2 but not Myo15ΔN/ΔN (Figure 2A).

claim: Myo15ΔN/ΔN OHCs at P4 developed a normal hair bundle morphology that was clearly distinct from age-matched Myo15sh2/sh2 OHCs.
source: Similar to IHCs, Myo15ΔN/ΔN OHCs at P4 also developed a normal hair bundle morphology that was clearly distinct from age-matched Myo15sh2/sh2 OHCs (Figure 2B).
evidence: SEM images showing normal OHC bundle morphology in Myo15ΔN/ΔN compared to Myo15sh2/sh2 (Figure 2B).

claim: Hair bundles of IHCs and OHCs initially developed normally at P4 but subsequently degenerated.
source: Although the hair bundles of IHCs and OHCs initially developed normally at P4, they subsequently degenerated (Figure 6), and this likely contributes to the deafness observed in Myo15ΔN/ΔN mice at P14 and older (Figure 1C).
evidence: SEM showing normal morphology at P4 (Figure 2) and degeneration at later ages (Figure 6).

claim: Isoform 1 was concentrated at the tips of the shorter second and third row stereocilia in P14 IHC bundles.
source: Labeling of P14 IHC bundles with PB888 (Figure 3A) and PB886 (data not shown) revealed that isoform 1 was concentrated at the tips of the shorter second and third row stereocilia.
evidence: Immunofluorescence with isoform 1-specific antibodies showing localization to shorter rows (Figure 3A).

claim: Isoform 1 was inconsistently detected at the tips of the tallest row in IHCs.
source: Isoform 1 was inconsistently detected at the tips of the tallest row, with (data not shown), or without antigen retrieval (Figure 3—figure supplement 1F), indicating that the asymmetric distribution in stereocilia rows was unlikely due to epitope masking.
evidence: Immunofluorescence showing variable detection on tallest row (Figure 3—figure supplement 1F).

claim: Gold particles were concentrated within the prolate tips of wild-type shorter stereocilia of P16 IHCs.
source: Gold particles were concentrated within the prolate tips of wild-type shorter stereocilia of P16 IHCs (Figure 3C,D) and were infrequently observed along the stereocilia core (Figure 3C).
evidence: Immuno-TEM showing gold particle localization at stereocilia tips (Figure 3C,D).

claim: Isoform 1 was not detected at the upper tip-link insertion site on the tallest row in mechanically splayed IHC bundles.
source: Consistent with this, isoform 1 was not detected at the upper tip-link insertion site on the tallest row in mechanically splayed IHC bundles (Figure 3F).
evidence: Immunofluorescence of splayed bundles showing no signal at upper tip-link insertion (Figure 3F).

claim: In OHCs at P14, isoform 1 was detected at the tips of shorter stereocilia and additionally at the tips of the tallest row.
source: In OHCs at P14, isoform 1 was similarly detected at the tips of shorter stereocilia (Figure 3B,E) but additionally at the tips of the tallest row (Figure 3B,B′).
evidence: Immunofluorescence showing isoform 1 on all rows in OHCs (Figure 3B,B′).

claim: Isoform 1 localizes to the tip density of shorter row stereocilia in close proximity to the site of MET.
source: We conclude that isoform 1 localizes to the tip density of shorter row stereocilia in close proximity to the site of MET (Beurg et al., 2009).
evidence: Immunofluorescence and immuno-TEM data showing localization to shorter row tips (Figure 3), combined with knowledge that MET channels are at shorter row tips (Beurg et al., 2009).

claim: Similar localization patterns of isoform 1 were observed from P7 through to P28 in both IHCs and OHCs.
source: Similar localization patterns of isoform 1 were observed not only at P14 (Figure 3A,B) but also from P7 through to P28 in both IHCs and OHCs (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C,E), indicating that this was the distribution of isoform 1 in mature hair cells.
evidence: Immunofluorescence at multiple developmental time points (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C,E).

claim: Only trace PB888 labeling was detected in stereocilia of hair cells at P1.
source: Only trace PB888 labeling was detected in stereocilia of hair cells at P1 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A), consistent with the relatively low abundance of isoform 1 transcripts detected at this age by qPCR (Figure 1F and Figure 1—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: Immunofluorescence showing minimal signal at P1 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A) consistent with qPCR data (Figure 1F).

claim: The apparent absence of isoform 1 in young hair bundles provides an explanation for why mutations of exon 2 do not affect stereocilia elongation or establishment of the hair bundle architecture.
source: The apparent absence of isoform 1 in young hair bundles provides an explanation for why mutations of exon 2 do not affect stereocilia elongation or establishment of the hair bundle architecture.
evidence: Immunofluorescence showing low isoform 1 at P1 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A) combined with normal bundle development in Myo15ΔN/ΔN mice (Figure 2).

claim: No stereocilia labeling was observed with PB888 or PB886 in mutant Myo15ΔN/ΔN cochleae.
source: We observed no stereocilia labeling with either PB888 or PB886, confirming antibody specificity and also that the Myo15ΔN allele resulted in the loss of isoform 1 from the hair bundle.
evidence: Immunofluorescence showing absence of signal in Myo15ΔN/ΔN hair cells (Figure 3G,H).

claim: A truncated isoform 1 could not localize to stereocilia without the motor and tail domains.
source: Since the premature stop codon (p.E1086X) did not trigger nonsense-mediated mRNA decay in Myo15ΔN/ΔN cochleae (Figure 1H), we hypothesized that a truncated isoform 1 could not localize to stereocilia without the motor and tail domains.
evidence: Inference based on presence of mRNA (Figure 1H) but absence of protein localization (Figure 3G,H).

claim: The actin-binding motor domain is critical to actively localize isoform 1 within stereocilia.
source: Consistent with this, PB888 labeling was absent from stereocilia of Myo15sh2/sh2 hair cells (Figure 3I), indicating that the actin-binding motor domain is critical to actively localize isoform 1 within stereocilia.
evidence: Immunofluorescence showing no isoform 1 localization in motor domain mutant (Figure 3I).

claim: PB48 strongly localized to tips of the tallest stereocilia row of littermate Myo15ΔN/ΔN IHCs at P7 and P14.
source: PB48 still strongly localized to tips of the tallest stereocilia row of littermate Myo15ΔN/ΔN IHCs, however there was a selective loss from the shorter (second and third) stereocilia rows at both P7 (Figure 4A) and P14 (Figure 4B).
evidence: Immunofluorescence showing PB48 signal on tallest row in Myo15ΔN/ΔN IHCs (Figure 4A,B).

claim: There was a selective loss of PB48 signal from the shorter stereocilia rows in Myo15ΔN/ΔN IHCs at P7 and P14.
source: PB48 still strongly localized to tips of the tallest stereocilia row of littermate Myo15ΔN/ΔN IHCs, however there was a selective loss from the shorter (second and third) stereocilia rows at both P7 (Figure 4A) and P14 (Figure 4B).
evidence: Immunofluorescence showing reduced PB48 signal on shorter rows in Myo15ΔN/ΔN IHCs (Figure 4A,B).

claim: In IHCs from normal controls at P7, the intensity of PB48 labeling on the second row was 54 ± 22% of the first row signal.
source: In IHCs from normal controls at P7, the intensity of PB48 labeling on the second row was 54 ± 22% (mean ± SD) of the first row signal (Figure 4C).
evidence: Quantitative fluorescence analysis of PB48 signal (Figure 4C).

claim: In Myo15ΔN/ΔN IHCs the PB48 intensity on second row was significantly reduced to 9.7 ± 5.9% of the tallest row intensity.
source: In Myo15ΔN/ΔN IHCs this values was significantly reduced to 9.7 ± 5.9% of the tallest row intensity (Figure 4C).
evidence: Quantitative fluorescence analysis showing reduced PB48 signal on second row in Myo15ΔN/ΔN (Figure 4C).

claim: The majority of myosin 15 in the second row is isoform 1 and isoform 2 is the minor species at this location.
source: This indicates that the majority of myosin 15 in the second row is isoform 1 and that isoform 2 is the minor species at this location.
evidence: Inferred from quantitative fluorescence showing large reduction in PB48 signal on second row when isoform 1 is absent (Figure 4C).

claim: Myosin 15 isoforms are sorted into different stereocilia rows as early as P7 in IHCs.
source: These observations, taken together with PB888 data, support the conclusion that myosin 15 isoforms are sorted into different stereocilia rows as early as P7 in IHCs.
evidence: Combined immunofluorescence data showing differential localization of isoforms 1 and 2 at P7 (Figures 3, 4).

claim: At P1, a strong PB48 signal was observed at the stereocilia tips of both IHCs and OHCs of isoform 1-null Myo15ΔN/ΔN mice that was comparable with the PB48 signal in control mice of the same age.
source: At P1, a strong PB48 signal was observed at the stereocilia tips of both IHCs and OHCs of isoform 1-null Myo15ΔN/ΔN mice that was comparable with the PB48 signal in control mice of the same age (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: Immunofluorescence showing similar PB48 signal in Myo15ΔN/ΔN and controls at P1 (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A,B).

claim: PB48 labeling persisted at the tallest row of Myo15ΔN/ΔN IHC stereocilia at P7 and P14.
source: Later in development, PB48 labeling persisted at the tallest row of Myo15ΔN/ΔN IHC stereocilia at P7 and P14 (Figure 4A,B) but was progressively diminished in Myo15ΔN/ΔN OHC stereocilia at P7 and P14 (Figure 4A and Figure 4—figure supplement 1C), as compared to the labeling in control OHCs from littermates (Figure 4A, Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Immunofluorescence showing PB48 signal on tallest row of IHCs at P7 and P14 (Figure 4A,B).

claim: PB48 labeling was progressively diminished in Myo15ΔN/ΔN OHC stereocilia at P7 and P14.
source: Later in development, PB48 labeling persisted at the tallest row of Myo15ΔN/ΔN IHC stereocilia at P7 and P14 (Figure 4A,B) but was progressively diminished in Myo15ΔN/ΔN OHC stereocilia at P7 and P14 (Figure 4A and Figure 4—figure supplement 1C), as compared to the labeling in control OHCs from littermates (Figure 4A, Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Immunofluorescence showing reduced PB48 signal in OHCs at P7 and P14 (Figure 4A, Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).

claim: The overall decline of isoform 2 mRNA detected by qPCR may originate from a change in OHC expression.
source: These observations suggest that the overall decline of isoform 2 mRNA detected by qPCR (Figure 1G) may originate from a change in OHC expression.
evidence: Inference based on reduced PB48 signal in OHCs (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C) and qPCR showing decline in isoform 2 (Figure 1G).

claim: There is a developmental transition from isoform 2 to isoform 1 by the time the mature hair bundle architecture is almost fully developed (i.e. by P6).
source: In summary, our data show a developmental transition from isoform 2 to isoform 1 by the time the mature hair bundle architecture is almost fully developed (i.e. by P6).
evidence: qPCR data showing isoform switching (Figure 1F,G) and immunofluorescence showing differential localization by P7 (Figures 3, 4).

claim: The independent segregation of myosin 15 isoforms within the hair bundle provides a mechanism for why the Myo15ΔN and Myo15sh2 alleles cause strikingly different hair bundle phenotypes.
source: Furthermore, the independent segregation of myosin 15 isoforms within the hair bundle provides a mechanism for why the Myo15ΔN and Myo15sh2 alleles cause strikingly different hair bundle phenotypes.
evidence: Inference based on differential localization of isoforms (Figures 3, 4) and different phenotypes of mutants (Figure 2).

claim: Isoform 2 is still present in stereocilia of Myo15ΔN/ΔN hair cells and is sufficient to drive hair bundle elongation.
source: Whilst both isoforms are absent from Myo15sh2/sh2 hair bundles, isoform 2 is still present in stereocilia of Myo15ΔN/ΔN hair cells and is sufficient to drive hair bundle elongation.
evidence: Immunofluorescence showing isoform 2 in Myo15ΔN/ΔN (Figure 4A,B) and normal bundle development (Figure 2).

claim: Isoform 1 has a function critical for hearing that is unrelated to stereocilia bundle development.
source: It follows that isoform 1 has a function critical for hearing that is unrelated to stereocilia bundle development.
evidence: Inference based on normal bundle development (Figure 2) but progressive deafness (Figure 1) in Myo15ΔN/ΔN mice.

claim: In normal Myo15+/ΔN cochleae, whirlin was concentrated at the tips of the tallest row of IHC and OHC stereocilia at both P7 and P14.
source: In normal Myo15+/ΔN cochleae, whirlin was concentrated at the tips of the tallest row of IHC and OHC stereocilia at both P7 and P14 (Figure 4D,E and Figure 4—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: Immunofluorescence showing whirlin localization in control hair cells (Figure 4D,E).

claim: The localization of whirlin in isoform 1-null Myo15ΔN/ΔN cochleae at both P7 and P14 was indistinguishable from their Myo15+/ΔN littermates.
source: When examined in isoform 1-null Myo15ΔN/ΔN cochleae at both P7 and P14, the localization of whirlin in IHCs and OHCs was indistinguishable from their Myo15+/ΔN littermates (Figure 4D,E and Figure 4—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: Immunofluorescence showing similar whirlin localization in Myo15ΔN/ΔN and controls (Figure 4D,E).

claim: Eps8 was detected at the tips of the tallest stereocilia row of control Myo15+/ΔN IHCs at both P7 and P14.
source: Similarly, Eps8 was detected at the tips of the tallest stereocilia row of control Myo15+/ΔN IHCs at both P7 and P14 (Figure 4F, Figure 4—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: Immunofluorescence showing Eps8 localization in control IHCs (Figure 4F, Figure 4—figure supplement 1E).

claim: In isoform 1-null Myo15ΔN/ΔN cochleae, Eps8 labeling in IHCs and OHCs appeared unchanged from the wild-type littermates.
source: In isoform 1-null Myo15ΔN/ΔN cochleae, Eps8 labeling in IHCs and OHCs appeared unchanged from the wild-type littermates (Figure 4F, Figure 4—figure supplement 1E,F,G).
evidence: Immunofluorescence showing similar Eps8 localization in Myo15ΔN/ΔN and controls (Figure 4F, Figure 4—figure supplement 1E,F,G).

claim: Isoform 2 by itself is sufficient to establish the wild-type distribution of Eps8 and whirlin in IHCs and OHCs.
source: We conclude that isoform 2 by itself is sufficient to establish the wild-type distribution of Eps8 and whirlin in IHCs and OHCs.
evidence: Immunofluorescence showing normal Eps8 and whirlin localization in isoform 1-null mice (Figure 4D-F).

claim: Whirlin and Eps8 bind to domains in the C-terminal tail of myosin 15 that are common to both isoforms 1 and 2.
source: Whirlin and Eps8 bind to domains in the C-terminal tail of myosin 15 that are common to both isoforms 1 and 2 (Belyantseva et al., 2005; Delprat et al., 2005; Manor et al., 2011).
evidence: Referenced from prior publications (Belyantseva et al., 2005; Delprat et al., 2005; Manor et al., 2011).

claim: The localization of whirlin and Eps8 do not depend upon isoform 1, despite the abundance of isoform 1 in hair bundles from P7 onwards.
source: It is striking therefore that the localization of whirlin and Eps8 do not depend upon isoform 1, despite the abundance of isoform 1 in hair bundles from P7 onwards.
evidence: Immunofluorescence showing normal whirlin and Eps8 localization in isoform 1-null mice (Figure 4D-F) despite isoform 1 expression from P7 (Figure 3).

claim: The apparent selectivity for isoform 2 explains how Eps8 and whirlin are primarily trafficked to the tallest stereocilia row.
source: The apparent selectivity for isoform 2 explains how Eps8 and whirlin are primarily trafficked to the tallest stereocilia row and why the ablation of isoform 1 does not interfere with stereocilia development in Myo15ΔN/ΔN cochleae.
evidence: Inference based on isoform 2 localization to tallest row (Figure 4A,B) and normal Eps8/whirlin localization in isoform 1-null mice (Figure 4D-F).

claim: Maximal MET current amplitudes were not statistically different between mutant Myo15ΔN/ΔN and control Myo15+/ΔN IHCs.
source: Maximal MET current amplitudes were not statistically different between mutant Myo15ΔN/ΔN (n = 12) and control Myo15+/ΔN IHCs (n = 10) (Figure 5E).
evidence: Electrophysiological recordings showing similar maximal MET currents (Figure 5E).

claim: The responses to small bundle deflections (150–300 nm) were significantly larger in mutant Myo15ΔN/ΔN IHCs, indicating an increased deflection sensitivity of the transduction apparatus in the absence of isoform 1.
source: However, the responses to small bundle deflections (150–300 nm) were significantly larger in mutant Myo15ΔN/ΔN IHCs, indicating an increased deflection sensitivity of the transduction apparatus in the absence of isoform 1 (Figure 5E).
evidence: Electrophysiological recordings showing larger responses to small deflections in Myo15ΔN/ΔN IHCs (Figure 5E).

claim: Isoform 1 is not essential for MET responses in IHCs but may contribute to the stiffness of the gating spring.
source: Our data show that isoform 1 is not essential for MET responses in IHCs but may contribute to the stiffness of this gating spring.
evidence: Electrophysiological data showing MET currents present but with altered sensitivity in Myo15ΔN/ΔN IHCs (Figure 5E).

claim: A similar increase of MET sensitivity was not observed in OHCs.
source: We did not observe a similar increase of MET sensitivity in OHCs (Myo15ΔN/ΔN, n = 9; Myo15+/ΔN, n = 7), perhaps due to the MET current degradation already present in Myo15ΔN/ΔN OHCs compared to Myo15+/ΔN controls (Figure 5H).
evidence: Electrophysiological recordings showing no increased sensitivity in OHCs (Figure 5H).

claim: The time constant of adaptation was not affected in either IHCs or OHCs of Myo15ΔN/ΔN mice compared to Myo15+/ΔN controls.
source: The time constant of adaptation was not affected in either IHCs or OHCs of Myo15ΔN/ΔN mice compared to Myo15+/ΔN controls (Figure 5F,I).
evidence: Electrophysiological measurements of adaptation time constants (Figure 5F,I).

claim: The extent of adaptation was identical in Myo15ΔN/ΔN and Myo15+/ΔN IHCs.
source: The extent of adaptation, represented as the percentage of the MET current decay during a step-like bundle deflection, was identical in Myo15ΔN/ΔN and Myo15+/ΔN IHCs (Figure 5G), and larger in Myo15ΔN/ΔN OHCs as compared to Myo15+/ΔN OHCs (Figure 5J).
evidence: Electrophysiological measurements of adaptation extent (Figure 5G).

claim: The extent of adaptation was larger in Myo15ΔN/ΔN OHCs as compared to Myo15+/ΔN OHCs.
source: The extent of adaptation, represented as the percentage of the MET current decay during a step-like bundle deflection, was identical in Myo15ΔN/ΔN and Myo15+/ΔN IHCs (Figure 5G), and larger in Myo15ΔN/ΔN OHCs as compared to Myo15+/ΔN OHCs (Figure 5J).
evidence: Electrophysiological measurements of adaptation extent (Figure 5J).

claim: Isoform 1 is not essential for assembling the MET machinery in early postnatal development, but can contribute to the overall stiffness of the MET apparatus.
source: We conclude that isoform 1 is not essential for assembling the MET machinery in early postnatal development, but can contribute to the overall stiffness of the MET apparatus.
evidence: Electrophysiological data showing MET currents present but with altered mechanical sensitivity in Myo15ΔN/ΔN hair cells (Figure 5).

claim: At P4 through P10, the gross morphology of Myo15ΔN/ΔN hair cells was similar to control Myo15+/ΔN littermates.
source: At P4 through P10, the gross morphology of Myo15ΔN/ΔN hair cells was similar to control Myo15+/ΔN littermates (Figure 6A,B, top row), consistent with isoform 2 being sufficient for stereocilia development.
evidence: SEM showing similar morphology in Myo15ΔN/ΔN and controls at P4-P10 (Figure 6A,B).

claim: In older Myo15ΔN/ΔN cochleae from P32 onwards, the mechanotransducing stereocilia in the second row were evidently reduced in height compared with normal hearing Myo15+/ΔN controls.
source: However, in older Myo15ΔN/ΔN cochleae from P32 onwards, the mechanotransducing stereocilia in the second row were evidently reduced in height compared with normal hearing Myo15+/ΔN controls.
evidence: SEM showing reduced second row stereocilia height in Myo15ΔN/ΔN at P32 (Figure 6A,B).

claim: The third stereocilia row was almost completely resorbed by P32 in Myo15ΔN/ΔN hair cells.
source: Furthermore, the third stereocilia row was almost completely resorbed by P32 in Myo15ΔN/ΔN hair cells.
evidence: SEM showing loss of third row stereocilia in Myo15ΔN/ΔN at P32 (Figure 6A,B).

claim: Degeneration was specific to the shorter rows that harbor active MET channels, and it did not affect the tallest rows, at least up until P50.
source: Remarkably, this degeneration was specific to the shorter rows that harbor active MET channels (Beurg et al., 2009), and it did not affect the tallest rows, at least up until P50.
evidence: SEM showing selective degeneration of shorter rows but preservation of tallest row up to P50 (Figure 6A,B).

claim: The same degenerative phenotype was observed in Myo15ΔN/sh2-J compound heterozygotes.
source: The same degenerative phenotype was observed in Myo15ΔN/sh2-J compound heterozygotes, which produce normal isoform 2 from the Myo15ΔN allele and a mutant isoform 1 lacking the tail domain from the Myo15sh2-J allele (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: SEM showing similar degeneration in compound heterozygotes (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).

claim: A single genetic copy of isoform 2 is sufficient for the production of a normal hair bundle.
source: These data indicate that a single genetic copy of isoform 2 is sufficient for the production of a normal hair bundle (Table 1) and show that isoform 1 must be full-length to maintain shorter row stereocilia.
evidence: Genotype-phenotype analysis showing normal bundle development in heterozygotes (Table 1).

claim: Isoform 1 must be full-length to maintain shorter row stereocilia.
source: These data indicate that a single genetic copy of isoform 2 is sufficient for the production of a normal hair bundle (Table 1) and show that isoform 1 must be full-length to maintain shorter row stereocilia.
evidence: Compound heterozygote data showing degeneration when isoform 1 lacks tail domain (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).

claim: In the second row of Myo15ΔN/ΔN IHCs at P8, the shape of the normally prolate tips were frequently exaggerated and over-elongated compared to Myo15+/+ IHCs.
source: In the second row of Myo15ΔN/ΔN IHCs at P8, the shape of the normally prolate tips were frequently exaggerated and over-elongated (Figure 7B), compared to Myo15+/+ IHCs (Figure 7A).
evidence: SEM showing over-elongated tips in Myo15ΔN/ΔN IHCs at P8 (Figure 7B).

claim: Over-elongated tips were observed in Myo15ΔN/ΔN IHCs at P8, but not at P4.
source: We observed these over-elongated tips in Myo15ΔN/ΔN IHCs at P8, but not at P4 (Figure 7—figure supplement 3), suggesting this abnormality was not a developmental defect, but rather the abnormal maintenance of stereocilia in isoform 1-deficient hair cells.
evidence: Quantitative analysis of tip shape showing normal aspect ratios at P4 but increased at P8 (Figure 7—figure supplement 3).

claim: The over-elongated tips of Myo15ΔN/ΔN IHCs were filled with actin filaments, indicating that actin polymerization was dysregulated at this location.
source: The over-elongated tips of Myo15ΔN/ΔN IHCs were filled with actin filaments (Figure 7B), indicating that actin polymerization was dysregulated at this location.
evidence: TEM showing actin filaments in over-elongated tips (Figure 7B).

claim: The tip density was absent from the tips of young postnatal Myo15sh2/sh2 stereocilia.
source: In agreement with a previous report (Rzadzinska et al., 2004), we confirmed that the tip density was absent from the tips of young postnatal Myo15sh2/sh2 stereocilia (Figure 7—figure supplement 1E–I), supporting the role of this structure in stereocilia elongation and actin polymerization.
evidence: TEM showing absence of tip density in Myo15sh2/sh2 stereocilia (Figure 7—figure supplement 1E-I), consistent with prior report (Rzadzinska et al., 2004).

claim: A prominent tip density was detected at the tips of Myo15ΔN/ΔN stereocilia at P7, similar to littermate controls.
source: In contrast to Myo15sh2/sh2 stereocilia, a prominent tip density was detected at the tips of Myo15ΔN/ΔN stereocilia at P7, similar to littermate controls (Figure 7A,B and Figure 7—figure supplement 1A–D).
evidence: TEM showing tip density present in Myo15ΔN/ΔN stereocilia (Figure 7A,B and Figure 7—figure supplement 1A-D).

claim: Isoform 2 is necessary to form the tip density complex and drive stereocilia elongation.
source: These data are consistent with isoform 2 being necessary to form the tip density complex and drive stereocilia elongation.
evidence: Inference based on tip density present in Myo15ΔN/ΔN (which has isoform 2) but absent in Myo15sh2/sh2 (which lacks both isoforms) (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).

claim: Isoform 1 is not required for initial tip density formation, but its incorporation into the postnatal structure appears to regulate actin dynamics, specifically on the shorter stereocilia rows that have active MET channels.
source: Whilst isoform 1 is not required for initial tip density formation, its incorporation into the postnatal structure appears to regulate actin dynamics, specifically on the shorter stereocilia rows that have active MET channels.
evidence: Inference based on tip density present in Myo15ΔN/ΔN (Figure 7A,B) but dysregulated actin dynamics evidenced by over-elongated tips (Figure 7B) and subsequent degeneration (Figure 6).

claim: Ablation of isoform 1 resulted in deterioration of the staircase architecture of the IHC bundle from P6 onwards.
source: In further support of this idea, ablation of isoform 1 resulted in deterioration of the staircase architecture of the IHC bundle from P6 onwards (Figure 7—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Quantitative measurements showing changes in stereocilia heights from P6 onwards (Figure 7—figure supplement 2).

claim: There was a clear reduction in second row stereocilia widths measured between P8 to P11 in Myo15ΔN/ΔN IHCs.
source: In addition, we observed a clear reduction in second row stereocilia widths measured between P8 to P11 in Myo15ΔN/ΔN IHCs (Figure 7E).
evidence: Quantitative measurements of stereocilia diameters showing reduction from P8 to P11 (Figure 7E).

claim: At P8, the distribution of diameters in the second stereocilia row of Myo15ΔN/ΔN IHCs was comparable to controls, although there was a small, statistically significant reduction in the average diameter.
source: At P8, the distribution of diameters in the second stereocilia row of Myo15ΔN/ΔN IHCs was comparable to controls (Figure 7E), although there was a small, statistically significant reduction in the average diameter (Figure 7F).
evidence: Quantitative measurements showing similar distribution but slightly reduced average diameter at P8 (Figure 7E,F).

claim: By P11, the average diameter of second row stereocilia in Myo15ΔN/ΔN hair cells was significantly reduced from 256 ± 2 nm to 189 ± 4 nm and included a distinct population of 'super-thin' stereocilia with diameters of less than 150 nm.
source: By P11, the average diameter of second row stereocilia in Myo15ΔN/ΔN hair cells was significantly reduced from 256 ± 2 nm (mean ± SEM) to 189 ± 4 nm and included a distinct population of 'super-thin' stereocilia with diameters of less than 150 nm (Figure 7E,F).
evidence: Quantitative measurements showing reduced diameter and super-thin population at P11 (Figure 7E,F).

claim: The diameter of the tallest stereocilia row did not decrease between P8 and P11 in IHCs.
source: In contrast, the diameter of the tallest stereocilia row did not decrease between P8 and P11 in IHCs (Figure 7F).
evidence: Quantitative measurements showing stable diameter of tallest row (Figure 7F).

claim: Stereocilia thinning was specific to Myo15ΔN/ΔN IHCs as shorter row stereocilia in OHCs of the same mutant mice retracted without any noticeable changes in diameter.
source: Stereocilia thinning was specific to Myo15ΔN/ΔN IHCs as shorter row stereocilia in OHCs of the same mutant mice retracted without any noticeable changes in diameter (Figure 6B, bottom row).
evidence: SEM showing retraction without thinning in OHCs (Figure 6B).

claim: TEM cross-sections revealed a similar density of actin filaments in normal and thinned stereocilia from Myo15+/+ and Myo15ΔN/ΔN IHCs at P28.
source: TEM cross-sections taken towards the base of the stereocilia core revealed a similar density of actin filaments in normal and thinned stereocilia from Myo15+/+ and Myo15ΔN/ΔN IHCs at P28 (Figure 7C,D).
evidence: TEM showing similar actin filament density in cross-sections (Figure 7C,D).

claim: Stereocilia thinning in Myo15ΔN/ΔN IHCs was caused by the loss of core actin filaments, rather than by an increased density of actin filament packing.
source: We infer that stereocilia thinning in Myo15ΔN/ΔN IHCs was caused by the loss of core actin filaments, rather than by an increased density of actin filament packing.
evidence: Inference based on reduced diameter but similar actin filament density (Figure 7C-F).

claim: Isoform 1 is required for the postnatal maintenance of the actin cytoskeleton, specifically in shorter row mechanotransducing stereocilia.
source: We conclude that isoform 1 is required for the postnatal maintenance of the actin cytoskeleton, specifically in shorter row mechanotransducing stereocilia.
evidence: Data showing selective degeneration of shorter rows (Figure 6), thinning (Figure 7E,F), and dysregulated actin dynamics (Figure 7B) in isoform 1-null mice.

claim: Mutations in Myo15 cause deafness through two fundamentally different mechanisms: (i) a failure to initially develop mechanosensory hair bundles, or (ii) a failure to maintain them once assembled.
source: We demonstrate that mutations in Myo15 cause deafness through two fundamentally different mechanisms: (i) a failure to initially develop mechanosensory hair bundles, or (ii) a failure to maintain them once assembled.
evidence: Comparison of Myo15sh2/sh2 (developmental defect, Figure 2) and Myo15ΔN/ΔN (maintenance defect, Figures 2, 6) phenotypes.

claim: The involvement of myosin 15 isoform 2 in stereocilia development was previously established.
source: The involvement of myosin 15 isoform 2 in stereocilia development was previously established (Belyantseva et al., 2005), however our finding that isoform 1 is required to maintain mature stereocilia was unexpected.
evidence: Referenced from prior publication (Belyantseva et al., 2005).

claim: The finding that isoform 1 is required to maintain mature stereocilia was unexpected.
source: The involvement of myosin 15 isoform 2 in stereocilia development was previously established (Belyantseva et al., 2005), however our finding that isoform 1 is required to maintain mature stereocilia was unexpected.
evidence: Novel finding from this study showing maintenance role of isoform 1 (Figures 6, 7).

claim: Myosin 15 isoforms can selectively traffic to different stereocilia rows and establish the distribution of other proteins (e.g., whirlin and Eps8) critical for stereocilia development.
source: Our study shows that myosin 15 isoforms can selectively traffic to different stereocilia rows and establish the distribution of other proteins (e.g., whirlin and Eps8) critical for stereocilia development.
evidence: Immunofluorescence showing differential isoform localization (Figures 3, 4) and normal whirlin/Eps8 distribution in isoform 1-null mice (Figure 4D-F).

claim: The unique N-terminal extension of isoform 1 must be responsible for regulating its ultimate destination within the hair bundle.
source: Because isoform 2 has no unique sequence when compared with isoform 1, the unique N-terminal extension of isoform 1 must be responsible for regulating its ultimate destination within the hair bundle.
evidence: Logical inference based on molecular structure (Figure 1A) and differential localization (Figures 3, 4).

claim: The shaker 2 (p.C1779Y) mutation within the actin-binding motor domain prevents both isoforms from accumulating in stereocilia.
source: The shaker 2 (p.C1779Y) mutation within the actin-binding motor domain prevents both isoforms from accumulating in stereocilia, and indicates that the interaction with actin is likely critical in the trafficking process.
evidence: Immunofluorescence showing no isoform 1 localization in Myo15sh2/sh2 (Figure 3I).

claim: The interaction with actin is likely critical in the trafficking process of myosin 15 isoforms.
source: The shaker 2 (p.C1779Y) mutation within the actin-binding motor domain prevents both isoforms from accumulating in stereocilia, and indicates that the interaction with actin is likely critical in the trafficking process.
evidence: Inference based on motor domain mutation preventing localization (Figure 3I).

claim: Stereocilia and rootlets contain a plethora of actin-binding proteins that may provide guidance cues to spatially regulate the activity of myosin 15 isoforms.
source: Although row-specific variations in actin topology have not yet been identified (Tilney et al., 1983), stereocilia and rootlets contain a plethora of actin-binding proteins that may provide guidance cues to spatially regulate the activity of myosin 15 isoforms (Drummond et al., 2012; Shin et al., 2013; Kitajiri et al., 2010).
evidence: Referenced from prior publications (Drummond et al., 2012; Shin et al., 2013; Kitajiri et al., 2010) and general knowledge of stereocilia composition.

claim: Eps8 and whirlin do not require isoform 1 to traffic to their normal locations within the hair bundle.
source: We found that Eps8 and whirlin do not require isoform 1 to traffic to their normal locations within the hair bundle.
evidence: Immunofluorescence showing normal Eps8 and whirlin localization in isoform 1-null mice (Figure 4D-F).

claim: The sole dependence of Eps8 and whirlin upon isoform 2 is intriguing since both myosin 15 isoforms share identical Eps8 and whirlin binding sites in the tail domain.
source: The sole dependence upon isoform 2 is intriguing since both myosin 15 isoforms share identical Eps8 and whirlin binding sites in the tail domain (Liang et al., 1999; Belyantseva et al., 2005; Manor et al., 2011).
evidence: Referenced from prior publications (Liang et al., 1999; Belyantseva et al., 2005; Manor et al., 2011) and molecular structure (Figure 1A).

claim: A distinct possibility is that the N-terminal extension may interact with the tail domain of myosin 15 to regulate binding to cargo proteins.
source: The molecular basis for this selectivity is unknown, although a distinct possibility is that the N-terminal extension may interact with the tail domain of myosin 15 to regulate binding to cargo proteins.
evidence: Speculation based on observed selectivity for isoform 2 in cargo trafficking (Figure 4D-F).

claim: Intra-molecular regulation is common in other myosin classes.
source: This type of intra-molecular regulation is common in other myosin classes (Sellers and Knight, 2007).
evidence: Referenced from prior publication (Sellers and Knight, 2007).

claim: Selective binding of cargo protein to isoform 1, or 2, forms the basis of a targeted protein trafficking system within mechanosensory hair bundles.
source: We postulate that selective binding of cargo protein to isoform 1, or 2, forms the basis of a targeted protein trafficking system within mechanosensory hair bundles.
evidence: Speculation based on differential isoform localization (Figures 3, 4) and cargo selectivity (Figure 4D-F).

claim: Isoform 1 may be responsible for trafficking proteins to the vicinity of the MET machinery on the shorter stereocilia rows.
source: Binding partners of the N-terminal extension are now of great interest, since isoform 1 may be responsible for trafficking proteins to the vicinity of the MET machinery on the shorter stereocilia rows.
evidence: Speculation based on isoform 1 localization to shorter rows (Figure 3) where MET channels are located.

claim: Exogenous expression of isoform 2 does not cause additional elongation of developing stereocilia in vitro.
source: This model is supported by the fact that exogenous expression of isoform 2 does not cause additional elongation of developing stereocilia in vitro (Belyantseva et al., 2003).
evidence: Referenced from prior publication (Belyantseva et al., 2003).

claim: Although isoform 1-null Myo15∆N/∆N hair cells have a reduced quantity of myosin 15 on their shorter stereocilia rows, no gross change in the initial development of the staircase architecture was observed.
source: We found that although isoform 1-null Myo15∆N/∆N hair cells have a reduced quantity of myosin 15 on their shorter stereocilia rows (Figure 4C), no gross change in the initial development of the staircase architecture was observed (Figure 7—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Quantitative fluorescence showing reduced myosin 15 (Figure 4C) but normal architecture (Figure 7—figure supplement 2).

claim: The data argue against the hypothesis that myosin 15 'dose' controls the length of individual stereocilia.
source: These data argue against the hypothesis that myosin 15 'dose' controls the length of individual stereocilia.
evidence: Inference based on reduced myosin 15 but normal stereocilia lengths (Figures 4C, 7—figure supplement 2).

claim: Isoform 1 is dispensable for the normal elongation of stereocilia in young postnatal hair cells.
source: Isoform 1 is dispensable for the normal elongation of stereocilia in young postnatal hair cells; by inference, we conclude that isoform 2 is sufficient to drive stereocilia development.
evidence: Data showing normal bundle development in isoform 1-null mice (Figure 2).

claim: Isoform 2 is sufficient to drive stereocilia development.
source: Isoform 1 is dispensable for the normal elongation of stereocilia in young postnatal hair cells; by inference, we conclude that isoform 2 is sufficient to drive stereocilia development.
evidence: Inference based on normal bundle development in isoform 1-null mice which retain isoform 2 (Figure 2).

claim: Myo15sh2/sh2 hair cells have short stereocilia where the actin core fails to elongate.
source: There is growing experimental evidence that myosin 15 regulates the actin cytoskeleton in developing stereocilia: (i) Myo15sh2/sh2 hair cells have short stereocilia where the actin core fails to elongate (Probst et al., 1998); (ii) exogenous expression of isoform 2 in Myo15sh2/sh2 hair cells rescues elongation of the stereocilia core, which entails actin polymerization (Belyantseva et al., 2005); (iii) expression of isoform 2 in COS-7 cells induces filopodia formation, again entailing actin polymerization (Belyantseva et al., 2003); (iv) our present study shows that the loss of isoform 1 results in progressive disassembly of mature mechanotransducing stereocilia.
evidence: Referenced from prior publication (Probst et al., 1998).

claim: Exogenous expression of isoform 2 in Myo15sh2/sh2 hair cells rescues elongation of the stereocilia core, which entails actin polymerization.
source: There is growing experimental evidence that myosin 15 regulates the actin cytoskeleton in developing stereocilia: (i) Myo15sh2/sh2 hair cells have short stereocilia where the actin core fails to elongate (Probst et al., 1998); (ii) exogenous expression of isoform 2 in Myo15sh2/sh2 hair cells rescues elongation of the stereocilia core, which entails actin polymerization (Belyantseva et al., 2005); (iii) expression of isoform 2 in COS-7 cells induces filopodia formation, again entailing actin polymerization (Belyantseva et al., 2003); (iv) our present study shows that the loss of isoform 1 results in progressive disassembly of mature mechanotransducing stereocilia.
evidence: Referenced from prior publication (Belyantseva et al., 2005).

claim: Expression of isoform 2 in COS-7 cells induces filopodia formation, entailing actin polymerization.
source: There is growing experimental evidence that myosin 15 regulates the actin cytoskeleton in developing stereocilia: (i) Myo15sh2/sh2 hair cells have short stereocilia where the actin core fails to elongate (Probst et al., 1998); (ii) exogenous expression of isoform 2 in Myo15sh2/sh2 hair cells rescues elongation of the stereocilia core, which entails actin polymerization (Belyantseva et al., 2005); (iii) expression of isoform 2 in COS-7 cells induces filopodia formation, again entailing actin polymerization (Belyantseva et al., 2003); (iv) our present study shows that the loss of isoform 1 results in progressive disassembly of mature mechanotransducing stereocilia.
evidence: Referenced from prior publication (Belyantseva et al., 2003).

claim: The loss of isoform 1 results in progressive disassembly of mature mechanotransducing stereocilia.
source: There is growing experimental evidence that myosin 15 regulates the actin cytoskeleton in developing stereocilia: (i) Myo15sh2/sh2 hair cells have short stereocilia where the actin core fails to elongate (Probst et al., 1998); (ii) exogenous expression of isoform 2 in Myo15sh2/sh2 hair cells rescues elongation of the stereocilia core, which entails actin polymerization (Belyantseva et al., 2005); (iii) expression of isoform 2 in COS-7 cells induces filopodia formation, again entailing actin polymerization (Belyantseva et al., 2003); (iv) our present study shows that the loss of isoform 1 results in progressive disassembly of mature mechanotransducing stereocilia.
evidence: Data from this study showing stereocilia degeneration in isoform 1-null mice (Figures 6, 7).

claim: The postnatal incorporation of isoform 1 into the tip density, along with its cargoes, may repurpose the actin polymerization machinery from driving elongation towards the fine-tuning of local actin dynamics.
source: However, once stereocilia are assembled, the postnatal incorporation of isoform 1 into the tip density, along with its cargoes, may repurpose the actin polymerization machinery from driving elongation towards the fine-tuning of local actin dynamics; which are normally restricted to the tips of mature stereocilia (Zhang et al., 2012; Drummond et al., 2015; Narayanan et al., 2015).
evidence: Speculation based on isoform 1 localization to tip density (Figure 3) and known actin dynamics at stereocilia tips (Zhang et al., 2012; Drummond et al., 2015; Narayanan et al., 2015).

claim: The onset of stereocilia abnormalities in the second row and changes to the staircase architecture occur around the same time as the appearance of isoform 1 within normal hair bundles (i.e. by P7).
source: Accordingly, we note that the onset of stereocilia abnormalities in the second row (Figure 7—figure supplement 3) and changes to the staircase architecture (Figure 7—figure supplement 2) occur around the same time as the appearance of isoform 1 within normal hair bundles (i.e. by P7).
evidence: Temporal correlation between isoform 1 appearance (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C) and onset of abnormalities (Figure 7—figure supplements 2, 3).

claim: The selective degeneration of only mechanotransducing stereocilia in Myo15∆N/∆N hair cells may result from the previously hypothesized link between MET currents and actin polymerization.
source: The selective degeneration of only mechanotransducing stereocilia in Myo15∆N/∆N hair cells may result from the previously hypothesized link between MET currents and actin polymerization (Tilney et al., 1988).
evidence: Speculation based on selective degeneration of shorter rows (Figure 6) and prior hypothesis (Tilney et al., 1988).

claim: The tallest stereocilia rows do not degenerate in Myo15∆N/∆N hair cells, since MET currents are not detected on the tallest rows.
source: This is consistent with the tallest stereocilia rows not degenerating in Myo15∆N/∆N hair cells, since MET currents are not detected on the tallest rows (Beurg et al., 2009).
evidence: Data showing preservation of tallest row (Figure 6) and knowledge that MET is not on tallest row (Beurg et al., 2009).

claim: A role for mechano-transduction has been further evidenced in hair cells of mutant Ush1gflox/flox mice, which lose tip-links and MET currents prior to degeneration of the shorter row stereocilia.
source: A role for mechano-transduction has been further evidenced in hair cells of mutant Ush1gflox/flox mice, which lose tip-links and MET currents prior to degeneration of the shorter row stereocilia (Caberlotto et al., 2011).
evidence: Referenced from prior publication (Caberlotto et al., 2011).

claim: The absence of MET currents was unlikely the cause of stereocilia disassembly in Myo15∆N/∆N hair cells, since grossly normal transduction was found in these cells.
source: Furthermore, the absence of MET currents was unlikely the cause of stereocilia disassembly in Myo15∆N/∆N hair cells, since we found grossly normal transduction in these cells.
evidence: Electrophysiological data showing MET currents present in Myo15∆N/∆N hair cells (Figure 5).

claim: Membrane tension is a critical factor controlling actin polymerization at the tips of mature mechanosensitive stereocilia.
source: We argue that membrane tension is instead a critical factor controlling actin polymerization at the tips of mature mechanosensitive stereocilia (Diz-Munoz et al., 2013; Barr-Gillespie, 2015) and that isoform 1 may contribute to a tension-sensing mechanism.
evidence: Referenced from prior publications (Diz-Munoz et al., 2013; Barr-Gillespie, 2015) and speculation based on current findings.

claim: Isoform 1 may contribute to a tension-sensing mechanism.
source: We argue that membrane tension is instead a critical factor controlling actin polymerization at the tips of mature mechanosensitive stereocilia (Diz-Munoz et al., 2013; Barr-Gillespie, 2015) and that isoform 1 may contribute to a tension-sensing mechanism.
evidence: Speculation based on isoform 1 localization to mechanosensitive stereocilia (Figure 3) and altered MET sensitivity (Figure 5E).

claim: The selective degeneration of shorter mechanotransducing stereocilia in Myo15∆N/∆N hair cells is reminiscent of the phenotype described in Ush1g, Tmhs, Eps8L2, Xirp2, Fscn2, Dstn, Wdr1 and Pls1 mouse mutants.
source: The selective degeneration of shorter mechanotransducing stereocilia in Myo15∆N/∆N hair cells is reminiscent of the phenotype described in Ush1g, Tmhs, Eps8L2, Xirp2, Fscn2, Dstn, Wdr1 and Pls1 mouse mutants (Caberlotto et al., 2011; Xiong et al., 2012; Furness et al., 2013; Perrin et al., 2013; Francis et al., 2015; Narayanan et al., 2015; Scheffer et al., 2015; Taylor et al., 2015).
evidence: Referenced from multiple prior publications showing similar phenotypes in other mutants.

claim: Isoform 1 may be part of a larger macromolecular complex, or signaling pathway, that maintains shorter row stereocilia with active MET channels.
source: Our observations allude to isoform 1 being part of a larger macromolecular complex, or signaling pathway, that maintains shorter row stereocilia with active MET channels.
evidence: Speculation based on similar phenotypes in multiple mutants and isoform 1 localization to shorter rows.

claim: The 133-kDa N-terminal extension, unique to isoform 1, contains dense clusters of poly-proline helices that are ligands for SH3, WW and Enabled/VASP homology (EVH1) domains commonly found in actin-regulatory proteins.
source: One possibility is that isoform 1 traffics components of a tension-sensing mechanism directly to the MET machinery. The 133-kDa N-terminal extension, unique to isoform 1, contains dense clusters of poly-proline helices (data not shown) that are ligands for SH3, WW and Enabled/VASP homology (EVH1) domains commonly found in actin-regulatory proteins.
evidence: Sequence analysis of N-terminal extension showing poly-proline helices.

claim: The N-terminal extension may interact with a broad range of proteins capable of directly orchestrating cytoskeletal dynamics.
source: The N-terminal extension may thus interact with a broad range of proteins capable of directly orchestrating cytoskeletal dynamics.
evidence: Speculation based on presence of protein interaction motifs in N-terminal extension.

claim: The N-terminal extension is predicted as intrinsically disordered due to its high-proline content (16.8%) and low sequence complexity.
source: The N-terminal extension is predicted as intrinsically disordered due to its high-proline content (16.8%) and low sequence complexity (http://dis.embl.de; data not shown).
evidence: Computational prediction based on sequence composition.

claim: Intrinsically disordered domains can explore multiple structural conformations.
source: Intrinsically disordered domains can explore multiple structural conformations (Dunker et al., 2002), and in some cases act as entropic spring elements, such as the PEVK domains within the giant muscle protein, titin (Linke et al., 1998; Watanabe et al., 2002).
evidence: Referenced from prior publications (Dunker et al., 2002; Linke et al., 1998; Watanabe et al., 2002).

claim: Hair bundle deflection sensitivity was increased in isoform 1-null Myo15∆N/∆N IHCs, consistent with the alteration of a spring element within the MET machinery.
source: We found that hair bundle deflection sensitivity was increased in isoform 1-null Myo15∆N/∆N IHCs, consistent with the alteration of a spring element within the MET machinery.
evidence: Electrophysiological data showing increased deflection sensitivity (Figure 5E).

claim: The reversible unfolding of titin's PEVK domains during muscle extension is proposed to expose buried SH3 ligands and enable force-dependent biochemical signaling.
source: In a further parallel with the N-terminal extension, the reversible unfolding of titin's PEVK domains during muscle extension is proposed to expose buried SH3 ligands and enable force-dependent biochemical signaling (Ma et al., 2006).
evidence: Referenced from prior publication (Ma et al., 2006).

claim: If the N-terminus were mechano-sensitive, this may result in tension-dependent interactions with SH3, WW and EVH1 domains, and retention of isoform 1 at sites of mechanical stress.
source: If the N-terminus were similarly mechano-sensitive, this may result in tension-dependent interactions with SH3, WW and EVH1 domains, and retention of isoform 1 at sites of mechanical stress, e.g. in the vicinity of the lower tip-link insertion point on stereocilia.
evidence: Speculation based on analogy with titin and isoform 1 localization to mechanosensitive stereocilia.

claim: A mechano-sensitive N-terminal extension may explain the localization of isoform 1 to the tallest rows of OHC stereocilia, since the tips likely experience tension from their attachment to the tectorial membrane during sound-induced deflections.
source: A mechano-sensitive N-terminal extension may also explain the localization of isoform 1 to the tallest rows of OHC stereocilia, since the tips likely experience tension from their attachment to the tectorial membrane during sound-induced deflections.
evidence: Speculation based on isoform 1 localization in OHCs (Figure 3B) and knowledge of OHC mechanics.

claim: Each hair bundle is composed of actin-based stereocilia that are arranged into rows of increasing height to create a staircase-like architecture.
source: Each hair bundle is composed of actin-based stereocilia that are arranged into rows of increasing height to create a staircase-like architecture; a feature evolutionarily conserved in vertebrates (Manley, 2000).
evidence: General knowledge of hair bundle structure referenced from prior publication (Manley, 2000).

claim: Extracellular tip-link filaments connect the tip of each stereocilium to the lateral shaft of its taller neighbor.
source: Extracellular tip-link filaments connect the tip of each stereocilium to the lateral shaft of its taller neighbor (Pickles et al., 1984).
evidence: General knowledge of tip-link structure referenced from prior publication (Pickles et al., 1984).

claim: Mechanotransducer ion channels are located at the tips of shorter rows of stereocilia.
source: Tensioning of these links during hair bundle deflection initiates mechanoelectrical transduction (MET) by gating mechanotransducer ion channels that are located at the tips of shorter rows of stereocilia (Beurg et al., 2009).
evidence: General knowledge of MET channel location referenced from prior publication (Beurg et al., 2009).

claim: Myosin 15 localizes to the tips of stereocilia, a site of barbed-end actin filament growth and turnover.
source: Myosin 15 localizes to the tips of stereocilia (Belyantseva et al., 2003; Rzadzinska et al., 2004; Belyantseva et al., 2005), a site of barbed-end actin filament growth and turnover (Schneider et al., 2002; Zhang et al., 2012; Drummond et al., 2015; Narayanan et al., 2015).
evidence: Referenced from multiple prior publications showing myosin 15 localization and actin dynamics at stereocilia tips.

claim: Myosin 15 is required for stereocilia elongation.
source: Myosin 15 is required for stereocilia elongation and traffics molecules to the stereocilia tips, including whirlin, a cytoskeletal scaffolding protein (Mburu et al., 2003; Belyantseva et al., 2005; Delprat et al., 2005), and epidermal growth factor receptor pathway substrate 8 (Eps8) which has actin binding, bundling and barbed-end capping activity (Disanza et al., 2004; Manor et al., 2011).
evidence: Referenced from multiple prior publications showing myosin 15 function in stereocilia elongation.

claim: Myosin 15 traffics whirlin to the stereocilia tips.
source: Myosin 15 is required for stereocilia elongation and traffics molecules to the stereocilia tips, including whirlin, a cytoskeletal scaffolding protein (Mburu et al., 2003; Belyantseva et al., 2005; Delprat et al., 2005), and epidermal growth factor receptor pathway substrate 8 (Eps8) which has actin binding, bundling and barbed-end capping activity (Disanza et al., 2004; Manor et al., 2011).
evidence: Referenced from prior publications (Mburu et al., 2003; Belyantseva et al., 2005; Delprat et al., 2005).

claim: Myosin 15 traffics Eps8 to the stereocilia tips.
source: Myosin 15 is required for stereocilia elongation and traffics molecules to the stereocilia tips, including whirlin, a cytoskeletal scaffolding protein (Mburu et al., 2003; Belyantseva et al., 2005; Delprat et al., 2005), and epidermal growth factor receptor pathway substrate 8 (Eps8) which has actin binding, bundling and barbed-end capping activity (Disanza et al., 2004; Manor et al., 2011).
evidence: Referenced from prior publications (Disanza et al., 2004; Manor et al., 2011).

claim: The loss of either whirlin or Eps8 recapitulates the short hair bundle phenotype and deafness of Myo15sh2/sh2 mice.
source: The loss of either whirlin or Eps8 recapitulates the short hair bundle phenotype and deafness of Myo15sh2/sh2 mice (Mburu et al., 2003; Belyantseva et al., 2005; Manor et al., 2011; Zampini et al., 2011), consistent with these proteins forming a complex with myosin 15 to promote stereocilia growth.
evidence: Referenced from multiple prior publications showing similar phenotypes in whirlin and Eps8 mutants.

claim: Alternative splicing creates two major protein isoforms from the 66 exon Myo15 gene.
source: Alternative splicing creates two major protein isoforms from the 66 exon Myo15 gene (Liang et al., 1999).
evidence: Referenced from prior publication (Liang et al., 1999) and molecular characterization (Figure 1A).

claim: Both isoform transcripts are detected in inner ear cDNAs and are expressed by hair cells.
source: Both isoform transcripts are detected in inner ear cDNAs (Belyantseva et al., 2003) and are expressed by hair cells (Liang et al., 1999; Anderson et al., 2000; Caberlotto et al., 2011).
evidence: Referenced from multiple prior publications showing expression of both isoforms.

claim: Mutations in exon 2 are associated with DFNB3 deafness in humans.
